title: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead
hook: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead; "the beginning of the good news"

segments.voice: Twenty-one days. Say them with me, fast: amen, grace, Jesus, the Lord's Prayer, the Sabbath, the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Beatitudes, love, the cross, Easter, the Psalms, faith, silence, communion, the church. Three weeks ago most of those were just words. Last day of Camp 1. Day twenty-one.
screen: the full strand, twenty words lit.

segments.voice: Every word you just said comes, one way or another, out of four short books: the Gospels. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. And the shortest of the four is Mark. Sixteen chapters. You could read the whole thing aloud in about two hours, in one sitting, the way the first Christians probably heard it: read out in somebody's house, start to finish. Most scholars think it's the oldest Gospel too, written down within about forty years of the events. It's fast. It's blunt. It skips the parts you'd expect. There's no Christmas in it, no shepherds, no star. It starts with a man shouting in the desert. And its very first line is today's word.
screen: `FOUR SHORT BOOKS.` → `MARK: THE SHORTEST.` → `NO CHRISTMAS. A DESERT.` → `THE FIRST LINE.`

segments.voice: Mark, chapter one, verse one. In the old King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." That's the whole verse. It's a title, and a door. Start with gospel. The English comes from the Old English godspel: good news. Mark's Greek word is euangelion, and it wasn't a church word yet. In the Roman world, a euangelion was a public announcement. A victory won. An emperor's birthday. News that changes the day for everyone who hears it. Mark takes that word and puts it on a carpenter from Galilee. Now, the shape, so you know the mountain ahead. First, Galilee: a man called by a river, fishermen dropping their nets, healings, arguments, and the stories he told. Mark's favorite word here is straightway. Immediately. Everything happens fast. Then, right in the middle, the turning point. Jesus asks his friends, who do you say that I am? And from there the road turns toward Jerusalem. The last third of the book is one week: the entry into the city, the table and the bread, the cross, and the empty tomb, where the oldest copies end with the women afraid. Which brings us back to the first word of the book. Beginning. Christians have noticed for a long time that Mark calls all of it, the whole book, just the beginning. As if the good news isn't finished when the book ends. As if the reader is supposed to pick it up from there. That's what the next camp does. Camp 2 is the stories: the ones he told, and the ones told about him. Start here.
screen: `EUANGELION — GOOD NEWS.` · `GALILEE: STRAIGHTWAY.` · `THE TURN: WHO DO YOU SAY I AM?` · `ONE LAST WEEK.` · then, large: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOOD NEWS.`

segments.voice: Last sit of the camp. Seventy-five seconds. Sit, and breathe, the way you did on day one. Remember the first word: amen. Let it be so. Now let one word from these three weeks come back to you on its own. Don't pick it. Let it arrive. Grace, maybe. Or the stone already moved. Or quiet. Hold it for a few breaths. Then ask yourself, gently: where does this start for me? If you pray, you can offer that word back as your prayer, with an amen. If you don't, just hold it, and let it be the beginning. The bell holds the time.
Mark 1:1. The beginning of the gospel. Good news, and only the beginning of it. Twenty-first word. And the strand is complete.
screen: `MARK 1:1 — your 21st word` → the strand complete → `CAMP 1. FIRST WORDS. DONE.`

segments.voice: Your line: start here. Tomorrow, Camp 2 begins: the stories. And it opens with a question: why did he tell stories at all? Twenty-one days. That's a practice. Day twenty-one.

howItsDone: Christians hear the Gospels read aloud in church, and many churches follow a cycle of readings in which one year is largely read from Mark. Some groups read the whole of Mark aloud in one sitting, the way it was likely first heard.

fork.setup: you're writing the first Gospel. everyone wants to know about this man. where do you begin?
options: with his birth in Bethlehem and a star.
with the beginning of the world.
with a man shouting in the desert, and a title: the beginning of the gospel.
fork.reveal: Mark skips the birth entirely. "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ" — and then straight into the desert. fast, blunt, no Christmas.

original.note: Greek, Mark 1:1: the beginning of the good news. the first words of the shortest Gospel.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chapter-and-verse number.
what it means: the first line of the shortest Gospel — a title that calls the whole book only the beginning of the good news.
what a scholar hears: euangelion was Roman imperial language for world-changing news. and some of the oldest manuscripts of Mark 1:1 have no "the Son of God" at all.

sources.quoted: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God

notes: Camp words in the review follow the index for days 1–20; days 4–8 (the Lord's Prayer, lines 1–5) are named once as 'the Lord's Prayer', so sixteen names are said for twenty words. The screen says 'twenty words lit.'
Mark as the oldest Gospel (Markan priority) and 'within about forty years' (c. AD 65–70) are the majority scholarly view, stated as 'most scholars think'. Some Christians hold Matthew was first.
'The Son of God' in Mark 1:1 is missing from some early manuscripts (e.g. the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus); mentioned only in the trapdoor.
KJV Mark 1:1 ends with a semicolon ('the Son of God;'); quoted without it.
Euangelion in imperial use (e.g. the Priene calendar inscription for Augustus's birthday) summarized without quotation.
Mark's frequent 'straightway / immediately' (Greek euthys, some forty times) given as his 'favorite word'; the KJV renders it variously (straightway, immediately, forthwith).
'Read aloud in about two hours' is an approximation.
Greek in 'original' is the opening phrase ἀρχὴ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου; pronunciation given in an Erasmian-leaning style — please check. Could instead be the single word εὐαγγέλιον.
Practice mentions 'the stone already moved' (day 15 carry) and 'quiet' (day 18) as examples.
